"This article is essentially an introduction to an interview with Jeffrey Eugenides, a well-known American novelist who wrote the Pulitzer Prize-winning book Middlesex. The piece opens with a quote from one of his stories, which suggests that learning more about your own country tends to reveal more reasons to feel ashamed of it. The writer of the article uses this quote to highlight a comparison between personal shame and national shame in America. Given that the article was written after major events like Hurricane Katrina, the 2008 financial crisis, and the election of Donald Trump following Barack Obama, the journalist wonders whether national shame now outweighs individual shame.

Eugenides responds that the two kinds of shame are roughly equal in weight. He points out that America has a history that includes slavery, which is a source of collective guilt. He also says that examining one's faults, whether personal or national, is a never-ending process. According to him, current events make it easier to focus on national problems, but personal struggles still matter. He explains that a nation is really just a collection of individuals, so national problems are also personal ones at their core. This creates a constant tension between how we see ourselves and how we see our country.

The setting of the interview is also described in the article, adding atmosphere and context. Eugenides is speaking from a library at Princeton University, where he has worked as a teacher for ten years. The building is brand new and not entirely finished, with a handwritten sign taped to a bathroom door marking it as unisex. This small detail serves to welcome readers into thinking about how university culture has shifted over the past decade. The journalist uses this to draw a parallel with broader social changes in America.

The article also mentions that Eugenides used to have to explain the meaning of the word intersex when promoting Middlesex years ago, which would not be necessary today.

* The article blends personal reflection with political commentary, touching on shame, identity, the health of American society, and how a writer like Eugenides processes these themes, perhaps even drawing from everyday relationships such as one between a boyfriend and girlfriend in his fiction.
* It also sets up the interview by describing the changing cultural landscape, showing how language around gender and identity has evolved rapidly and become part of mainstream conversation."
